notes.meaning: Paul and Barnabas arrived in Iconium and went straight to the Jewish meeting place, as they usually did. They spoke with such clarity and warmth that a large number of both Jews and Greeks believed in Jesus. God blessed their preaching with immediate fruit despite the hardships they had faced earlier.

Some of the Jewish hearers rejected the message and refused to believe. They stirred up the non-Jewish citizens and spread lies to turn their hearts against the new believers. Unbelief often tries to make others bitter and hostile toward the truth.

Instead of fleeing from the tension, the missionaries stayed there for a long time. They spoke boldly about the Lord Jesus, relying entirely on His strength rather than their own. The Lord confirmed their message of free grace by granting them power to perform miracles and wonders.

differ.view: Miracles and signs were not limited to the first apostles, but are still meant to confirm the preaching of the gospel today.
Miracles were special signs given only to establish the apostles' authority before the New Testament was completed.

notes.meaning: The message forced everyone in the city to take a stand. Some people sided with the opposing Jewish leaders, while others supported the apostles. Even the good news of Jesus can cause division when people refuse to accept it.

Opponents from both Jewish and non-Jewish backgrounds joined together with their local rulers. They formed a plan to insult the apostles publicly and stone them to death for their preaching. This was an unlawful mob attack rather than a legal court trial.

Paul and Barnabas learned of the plot and escaped before the mob could strike. They traveled south to the cities of Lystra and Derbe in the region of Lycaonia. Even while fleeing danger, they never paused in telling people the good news about Jesus.

In Lystra, they came across a man who had never walked a single step. He had been completely disabled in his feet from the day he was born. Because he could not move himself, he sat in public places where crowds gathered.

This man sat listening carefully while Paul preached the gospel. Paul looked straight at him and could tell that he had faith to be made whole. God often creates faith in the heart through the hearing of His word.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some faith healers teach that a sick person fails to get healed only because that person lacks enough personal faith.

notes.meaning: Paul called out in a loud voice and commanded the man to stand up straight. Without any hesitation, the man leaped up and began walking all around. His joyful jumping gave undeniable proof that his legs were fully healed by the Lord.

When the crowd saw this sudden cure, they began shouting in their local Lycaonian dialect. They believed their pagan gods had taken human form and come down to visit their town. A great miracle amazed them, but their hearts still clung to old superstitions.

The people named Barnabas after Zeus, the chief Greek god, likely because he appeared older and dignified. They called Paul Hermes, the messenger god, because he was the one doing all the preaching. They tried to squeeze God's miraculous work into their own mythological ideas.

The priest from the temple of Zeus, located just outside the city gate, brought bulls and flower garlands to the gates. He intended to lead the crowd in offering animal sacrifices to the two missionaries. The town was ready to treat ordinary men as objects of worship.

When Paul and Barnabas realized what was taking place, they tore their clothes in deep grief and shock. They ran straight into the middle of the crowd, shouting to stop the sacrifice. They cared far more about God's honor than any praise from men.

The apostles cried out that they were merely human beings who experience pain and weakness just like everyone else. They explained that their whole message was to urge people to turn away from worthless idols to the living God. This true God is the Creator who made the sky, the land, the sea, and everything alive.

In earlier generations, God allowed Gentile nations to live in their own chosen ways without giving them written Scripture. He showed great patience toward their ignorance rather than wiping them out immediately. Yet centuries of following bad customs never made their idolatry right.

Even without the Bible, God gave continuous evidence of His reality and kindness. He sends rain from the heavens, makes crops grow in their seasons, and provides plenty of food to bring gladness to people's hearts. Daily physical blessings are silent witnesses to God's generous love.

Even after reasoning with the crowd in this way, Paul and Barnabas could barely keep them from offering sacrifices. The people were so committed to their pagan habits that the truth was hard for them to grasp. It takes powerful grace to break people away from false worship.

Angry Jewish opponents traveled all the way from Antioch and Iconium to stir up trouble in Lystra. They swayed the fickle crowd, stoned Paul until he fell unconscious, and dragged him outside the walls, thinking he was dead. The very people who wanted to worship Paul as a god were quickly persuaded to murder him.

While the new disciples stood around Paul's battered body, he suddenly stood back up and walked into the city. God granted him an astonishing recovery from his wounds. The next day, he felt well enough to travel with Barnabas toward the town of Derbe.

In Derbe, they shared the good news and helped many people become disciples, meaning learners and followers of Jesus. Then they bravely retraced their steps back through Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch, where they had faced violence. They valued the safety of the new converts far more than their own comfort.

The apostles strengthened the minds of the new believers and urged them to remain steady in their faith. They taught honestly that every believer must pass through many hardships before entering the fullness of God's kingdom. Suffering for Christ is not a sign of failure, but part of the normal road to heaven.

Paul and Barnabas arranged for trusted leaders, called elders, to guide and care for each local congregation. They prayed and fasted together, committing these leaders and churches into the Lord's safe hands. Believers are always safest when entrusted directly to Christ.

differ.view: The local church members chose their own elders by voting, while the apostles guided the meeting.
Pastors were elected by the whole congregation's consent and officially set apart under the oversight of church leaders.

notes.meaning: Traveling onward, they crossed back through the province of Pisidia and came down into Pamphylia. They stopped to preach the message of Christ in the city of Perga, and then went on to the coastal port of Attalia. They made good use of every stop along the road to plant the word of God.

From the port of Attalia, they boarded a ship and sailed back to Antioch in Syria. This was the sending church that had prayed for them and entrusted them to God's grace at the start of their journey. They were returning home after successfully finishing the task God had assigned them.

Once back in Antioch, they gathered the whole congregation to give an account of their travels. They reported everything God had accomplished through them, especially how He had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles. They gave all the praise to God alone, knowing human preaching accomplishes nothing without His grace.

Paul and Barnabas settled down and stayed in Antioch for a long time with the other believers. After enduring long journeys, hard trials, and angry mobs, they enjoyed peaceful fellowship with Christian friends. Resting and sharing with the church renewed their strength for future ministry.
